title: Hewitt v. Hewitt
lead: An unmarried partner’s pleaded property-sharing claims were dismissed under the Illinois Supreme Court’s interpretation of the marriage policy embodied in the statutes then in force.

actors.name: Victoria Hewitt
actors.role: Plaintiff seeking half the accumulated property and profits

actors.name: Robert Hewitt
actors.role: Partner alleged to have promised a shared life, earnings, and property

proceedings: Circuit court: found no marriage and dismissed amended property claims.
Illinois Supreme Court: reversed appellate court and affirmed dismissal.
limits: This is the historical 1979 interpretation of Illinois’s statutory scheme, not current family-law advice. Claims about independent transactions between cohabitants and the children’s support rights were not categorically barred.

review.basis: Individually written and compared with the canonical full brief; no new independent opinion audit claimed.

sections.title: Victoria alleges a promise followed by fifteen years of shared family and professional effort
sections.cue: Introduce the asserted undertaking without treating it as a trial finding.
paragraphs: Victoria alleged that she and Robert Hewitt lived together from 1960 to 1975 and had three children. In June 1960, while both attended Grinnell College in Iowa, she became pregnant. According to her, Robert said they were husband and wife without a formal ceremony and promised to share his life, future, earnings, and property. They told their parents they were married and publicly presented themselves that way.

She alleged devotion to his professional education and pediatric dental practice, financial help from her parents, and contributions of her own skills. Payroll checks went into a common fund. She also provided homemaking, parenting, and social support for his professional reputation. She claimed he began without funds but through their efforts earned over $80,000 annually and accumulated substantial jointly or solely titled property. She sought half the profits and property from the relationship. These were allegations and described testimony, not findings that resolved the promise’s existence or terms.

sections.title: The original divorce request becomes four property theories
sections.cue: Trace the pleading stages and preserve child support separately.
paragraphs: Victoria first sued for divorce. At the dismissal hearing, she acknowledged no license or ceremony. The Champaign County circuit court found no ceremonial or common-law marriage. Because Robert admitted paternity, it said no separate Paternity Act action was needed to determine child support and directed specificity about claimed property. Support was not before the Supreme Court.

Her amendment asserted an express undertaking and joint efforts, an implied sharing agreement, a trust based on allegedly fraudulent assurances of marriage, and unjust enrichment from reliance and contributions. The circuit court dismissed, finding Illinois law and policy required a valid marriage for the property relief sought.

The appellate court reversed on an express oral agreement, emphasizing an outwardly conventional, respectable family life whose principal defect was absence of valid marriage. The Supreme Court granted review. It was deciding legal enforceability of the pleaded arrangement, not whether a sharing promise had been proved at trial.

sections.title: The court declines to treat the claim solely as ordinary contract enforcement
sections.cue: Explain its comparison to other approaches and the preserved exception.
paragraphs: Victoria argued that enforcing an actual bargain would not grant rights merely from cohabitation. The appellate court drew on Marvin, the California case recognizing express nonmarital agreements unless explicitly founded on sexual services and contemplating implied and equitable remedies. Justice Underwood noted that Marvin’s broad contract principle differed from an Illinois approach favoring only conventionally marriage-like households; the California claimant might fail that narrower respectability test.

More fundamentally, recognizing express agreements could lead to implied-contract, constructive-trust, and equitable litigation for relationships without explicit terms. The court viewed the change as implicating marriage, inheritance, support, children, and legal status, rather than only this private bargain. Its questions about consequences expressed concerns, not decisions on every collateral right.

Illinois precedent and traditional authorities rejected bargains for future illicit cohabitation or intercourse. The court acknowledged valid agreements on genuinely independent matters whose consideration excluded sexual relations and approaches elsewhere treating pooled earnings or domestic services as severable. It nevertheless declined to recharacterize this integrated marriage-like arrangement as an ordinary arm’s-length exchange. It did not void every commercial contract between people who happened to live together.

sections.title: The then-existing marriage statute supplies the majority’s policy inference
sections.cue: Present the statutory features and institutional choice.
paragraphs: Even if traditional doctrine should change, the court considered the legislature better equipped to assess sociological evidence and policy alternatives. The recently enacted Illinois Marriage and Dissolution of Marriage Act did not expressly address cohabitation, but the court inferred opposition to the claimed mutual property rights.

The Act promoted solemnization, registration, marriage preservation, and family protection. The court feared marriage-like property security could encourage a private alternative, possibly with arrangements unavailable to spouses. It also expressly preserved invalidity of Illinois common-law marriages after June 30, 1905. The alleged marital intent, assumed status, and public representation would have fit the former institution; equivalent property effects could indirectly restore what lawmakers abolished. A requested half share rather than actual spousal inheritance did not persuade the court.

The legislature’s then-recent retention of fault dissolution grounds, unlike California’s no-fault approach, further indicated its preference for marriage rather than a freely terminable private substitute. Putative-spouse protection required a ceremony and good-faith belief in validity, ended with knowledge of invalidity, and excluded common-law marriages. Adopted while Marvin was prominent, those limited protections seemed inconsistent with broad mutual property rights for knowingly unmarried couples. These were the court’s readings of the 1977 statutory scheme in 1979, not claims about current Illinois law.

sections.title: Dismissal stands without a finding that Victoria’s position lacked all merit
sections.cue: Give the exact disposition and historical limits.
paragraphs: The court expressly declined to dismiss Victoria’s position as wholly without merit. It nevertheless held the asserted property rights incompatible with policy implicit in the marriage legislation and left any broader change to the legislature.

On September 19, 1979, it reversed the appellate court and affirmed dismissal of the amended complaint. Underwood’s opinion contained no separate writing. It awarded Robert no damages and ordered no trial on an otherwise enforceable sharing agreement. The children’s support rights remained outside the issue.

Later approaches, including Watts and Restatement comparisons discussed in the assigned notes, were editorial comparisons rather than this judgment’s holdings. The opinion’s social concerns also were not empirical findings about every unmarried household.
